claims.text: Tungsten and CuCrZr components are intended for use in fusion reactor applications.
A W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf refractory high-entropy alloy can be used as an interlayer between W and CuCrZr.
The proposed W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf interlayer should be applied as a thin layer by deposition or cladding.
Fusion-reactor plasma-facing components can experience operating temperatures of at least 1000 K.
W-CuCrZr joints in divertor environments experience dynamic thermal cycling.
Fusion-reactor plasma-facing components are exposed to intense neutron irradiation.
The W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf HEA has a coefficient of thermal expansion intermediate between those of W and CuCrZr.
An interlayer with intermediate thermal expansion behavior reduces thermal stress at the W-CuCrZr interface.
Reduced interfacial thermal stress lowers the potential for cracking or delamination.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit high thermal stability and radiation resistance under extreme environments.
The specific W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf interlayer will retain radiation and thermal stability under fusion-reactor conditions.
Radiation and thermal stability of the interlayer will maintain the structural integrity of the W-CuCrZr joint.
The HEA-interlayer joint will have better thermal-cycling performance and lower residual stress than a joint without an interlayer.
The HEA-interlayer joint will develop fewer interfacial cracks or delaminations and have greater durability than a joint without an interlayer.
A directly joined W-CuCrZr interface is more susceptible to damage from thermal-expansion mismatch and irradiation.
Performance outside fusion-component design limits remains unverified.
The magnitude of stress reduction and long-term interlayer stability under cyclic irradiation and temperature fluctuations are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in interface stress and failure frequency relative to an interlayer-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
